chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from his brother al-Husayn ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn Yaqteen, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the man who prostrates on the leather sock (misaḥ) and the carpet, and he said, 'There is no harm if it is in a state of taqiyyah (prudent dissimulation/fear of harm).'

key_terms.الْمِسْحِ: the leather sock (used for dry ablution)
key_terms.تَقِيَّةٍ: prudent dissimulation or caution in religious practice

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to prostrate on a leather sock (misaḥ) during prayer according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the permissibility of prostrating on a leather sock (misaḥ) by linking it specifically to the context of *taqiyyah* (prudent dissimulation), a hallmark of Shia jurisprudence during periods of political pressure. While some schools view the material as a mere convenience, this hadith suggests the ruling is rooted in the necessity of maintaining ritual purity and validity when fear of persecution or loss of proper footwear exists. It highlights the Shia emphasis on the flexibility of fiqh to accommodate the believer's actual circumstances without compromising the sanctity of the prayer.
